title: Performance In Reality
excerpt: Performance in reality is the principle that product performance must be grounded in the real conditions, constraints and operational states in which a system is used. It contrasts with demo performance, theoretical performance and launch-day optimisation.
metaDescription: Definition of performance in reality: designing and evaluating products under the conditions that determine operational performance.
summary: Performance in reality is a recurring Creative Navy principle: products must be designed and evaluated against the concrete conditions that determine whether they work in operational use. The concept explains why systems can appear effective in demonstrations but fail under pressure, interruption, degraded states, high cognitive load and other real-use conditions.
definition: Performance in reality is the principle that product performance is concrete: it must be designed for and evaluated under the specific conditions, constraints and operational realities that determine whether a system works in actual use.
keyFacts: Performance in reality is a recurring principle rather than a single defined source term.
The principle contrasts with performance in demos, performance in theory and performance at launch.

Real operating conditions include pressure, interruption, edge cases, degraded states, high cognitive load, multi-role coordination, shift changes, time constraints, recoverable errors and unfamiliar scenarios.
The principle explains the failure pattern in which a product works in demos but not in real use.
User observation and domain learning are treated as necessary because real operating conditions cannot be designed for if they have not been observed or otherwise understood.
In the Torqeedo maritime HMI case, real operating conditions were documented and tested through 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains.
In the Triopsis workforce management SaaS case, live product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation and 58% faster weekly planning.

In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, real-route eye tracking recorded average glance duration falling from 4.32 seconds before redesign to 1.89 seconds after redesign under the same real conditions.

bodyMarkdown:
## Definition of performance in reality

Performance in reality is the principle that product performance is concrete. A product performs only under the specific conditions, constraints and operational realities that determine whether the system works in actual use.

In Creative Navy's documentation, the recurring framing is performance in reality, not performance in demos. The principle holds that products must be grown from reality to enable competitive performance, rather than derived from abstract best practices or assessed only in controlled presentations.

## What performance in reality is contrasted with

Performance in reality contrasts with three weaker forms of performance evidence.

Performance in demos refers to systems that work under controlled conditions but fail under real use. In a demo, users are not under operational pressure, edge cases do not appear, real cognitive load does not apply, workarounds are not visible, and the interface has not been used for an eight-hour shift.

Performance in theory refers to design derived from best practices rather than observed reality. The issue is not that best practices are irrelevant; the issue is that they cannot by themselves define the specific constraints of a real operating environment.

Performance at launch refers to optimisation for launch day rather than operational longevity. Performance in reality requires the design to survive the conditions that determine use after launch, not only the conditions present at handover.

## Real conditions that define operational performance

Performance in reality treats pressure, interruption, edge cases, degraded states, high cognitive load, multi-role coordination, shift changes, time constraints, recoverable errors and unfamiliar scenarios as design inputs. These conditions are not secondary details. They are often the conditions that determine whether the product actually works.

This is why user observation and domain learning matter in Creative Navy's documentation. A design team cannot design for real conditions it has not observed, reconstructed or otherwise understood. Performance in reality is also the operational expression of the infrastructure stewardship philosophy: infrastructure must work under real conditions.

## Why demo performance often fails in real use

A product can work in a demo and fail in real use because the demo removes the conditions that determine performance. Demonstrations often exclude pressure, interruption, degraded states, extended use, conflicting responsibilities, environmental variation and the need to recover from error.

The documented failure pattern is that the product works in demos but not in real use. Performance in reality explains why that pattern is common: demo conditions are controlled, while operational conditions are concrete, variable and consequential.

## Maritime HMI evidence from Torqeedo

In the Torqeedo maritime HMI case, the full range of real operating conditions was documented and tested against systematically. The case evidence describes 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains. The trials covered temperatures from −5°C to +35°C, night operations from late evening through early morning, vibration, sharp vessel movement, glare from cold water, rain and gloved touchscreen interaction.

These conditions were treated as normal operating conditions for professional maritime work, not as edge cases. The interface was designed for these conditions from the start rather than adapted for them after the fact.

Performance was evaluated under real maritime conditions. Comparative trials against the legacy interface found that captains identified key energy states 50% faster in a controlled experiment with 24 subjects. Glance counts during manoeuvres were measured using eye tracking in actual sea trials with 7 subjects.

## Workforce management evidence from Triopsis

In the Triopsis workforce management SaaS case, schedulers worked under peak load while handling weather incidents, conflicting job locations, overlapping assignments and sudden crew shortages simultaneously. Three in-situ observation sessions documented this operational reality before redesign decisions were made.

The redesign addressed those conditions directly. Predictive conflict indicators surfaced problems before users encountered them mid-task under pressure. Weather incidents, partial completions and delayed jobs were treated as normal workflow states rather than exceptional conditions requiring workarounds.

Performance was measured in the live product through product analytics. The documented results were 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation and 58% faster weekly planning, from real users in real operational conditions rather than usability testing tasks.

## Physical operating conditions in the Elsner smart home controller

In the Elsner smart home controller case, the controller was installed at 140cm height and used primarily in daylight, with evening use under limited luminance as a secondary context. These physical conditions were treated as design inputs.

Touch target sizing was calibrated to ergonomics research minimum dimensions and tested specifically for standing-height use. Automatic dark mode was a delivered behaviour of the shipped controller, triggered at sunset alongside the dual light and dark UI. The documented case evidence does not attribute that sunset trigger to a research method.

Sensor fault states, including delayed readings, contradictory values and calibration drift, were designed explicitly as normal operational conditions rather than as error cases. The interface was tested in prototype on actual hardware under real conditions, not only on screen simulations.

## Workshop performance evidence from Beissbarth

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration case, the conditions determining interface performance were not reproducible in a lab. Technicians read the embedded OEM display from 2–3 metres while moving around the vehicle. Gloves restricted fine touch interaction. Lighting varied, reflective surfaces reduced contrast, and the calibration sequence did not pause for interface interpretation.

Option space mapping variants were evaluated under reproduced workshop lighting and viewing distances, not on a screen at a desk. The outcome evidence is client-measured: calibration time fell from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 real deployment locations.

The Beissbarth evidence is field measurement from production deployments rather than usability testing data. It supports the narrower claim that the result survived contact with the actual conditions that determine performance in this domain.

## Deployment evidence from Gexcon CFD simulation software

In the Gexcon CFD simulation software case, engineers used the interface alongside a three-dimensional facility view. High-fidelity prototypes were tested in this configuration rather than in isolation, because the interaction model had to remain stable as attention shifted between the facility view, simulation parameters and system controls.

Non-linear workflows were normal operating conditions. Engineers moved between configuration, verification and interpretation without following a fixed path.

Performance was measured in real deployments. Time to first successful simulation fell from four days to six hours, and configuration errors per simulation fell from 5–8 to 1–2. Both figures come from operational deployment data rather than controlled testing.

## Longitudinal evidence from the Stromer e-bike embedded display

In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, the display was used while riding under variable conditions: urban streets, countryside terrain, varying light and weather. The rider's eyes had to leave the road to read the display, so controlled session testing would not reproduce the relevant operating condition.

Creative Navy designed the usability testing methodology around actual operating conditions. Ten participants rode the bike for 3 days each on real routes in Munich and surrounding countryside, logging issues on a 4-level severity scale. The 3-day duration was used to encounter the range of system states, warning types and terrain conditions that constituted actual use.

Eye tracking was also conducted during actual riding on the same routes. With 5 participants on the same terrain used in the usability test, average glance duration before the redesign was 4.32 seconds. The 2-second safety threshold cited from Klauer et al. (2006), NHTSA Report No. DOT HS 810 594, is derived from naturalistic driving study data. The post-redesign figure was 1.89 seconds under the same real conditions.

The Stromer case also includes a two-year follow-up using the same methodology. Warnings remained absent from the issues list. This is the strongest form of durability evidence in the documented set because the same instrument was applied two years after redesign under the same real-use methodology.

## Ecological testing evidence from Squaremind

In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device case, the core commercial promise was that patients could complete a full-body dermatology scan without clinical supervision. That claim was about performance in reality because clinics needed evidence that real patients of varying ages and physical literacy could complete the process unassisted in a real clinic environment.

An earlier improvised internal test by Squaremind produced 2 completions from 14 attempts. Creative Navy designed the post-redesign testing to match the conditions under which the commercial claim would have to hold.

Testing took place in two real locations: London with 12 users and Paris with 17 users. Participants received a free measurement as they would in an actual clinic, with no researcher guidance during the process. The sample was age-stratified across 20–35, 35–45 and 45–65. An independent dermatologist was hired by Creative Navy to co-conduct the sessions. Binary completion was the primary measure, and failure points and recovery times were catalogued.

The result was 27 of 29 independent completions and 12 of 12 recoveries among users who got stuck. The 29-user total was not a large sample by research standards, but the protocol produced ecological, age-stratified and clinically co-validated evidence before the device was taken to clinic demos. Nine clinics subsequently purchased the system, and Creative Navy attended 5 of the 9 demos as silent observers.

## Observed industrial-cell conditions against marketed automation conditions

In the industrial automation engagement, the client is described as a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells. The product is in development and not shipped.

The relevant contrast was between marketed cell automation and the observed reality at the client's facility. The observed cell had every operator screen bolted to its own machine, so the operator walked to each machine to learn its state. Overhead stack lights existed because no screen was readable across the hall. Work happened at standing height, with no seated station in the cell.

The observed facility also had mixed daylight through a glazed façade plus industrial ceiling light, strong side-light, glare and reflections, medium ambient noise from running machines, music playing, oil, coolant and metal swarf throughout, and aisles roughly one person wide. Entering the cell tripped the safety fence and stopped production, so every manual intervention carried a production cost.

These observations support the performance-in-reality point only for the client's facility. They should not be generalised as claims about the industry.

## Streetec kntrl 2 evidence from an actual product installed in a car

In the Streetec kntrl 2 case, testing took place after design work with the actual product installed in a car rather than a prototype on a desk. Creative Navy designed the test protocol, ran both sessions and analysed the results. Streetec prepared the vehicle and site logistics and recruited participants.

The two sessions included 32 participants total. Thirteen participants in Munich were tuning enthusiasts and car owners. Nineteen participants at a trade fair in Spain were mixed: roughly 25% owners or enthusiasts, 40% dealers, 30% installers and 5% other. The dealer and installer presence is relevant because dealers and installers commission and fit these systems.

All 32 participants completed all three tasks unassisted and performed in line with expectations. The supportable claim is limited to that completion finding. The Streetec evidence validated comprehension of a finished design in a parked car; it does not establish performance in use over time.

## AIT evidence from physical-size review and rotary-control constraints

In the AIT engagement, designs were reviewed at true physical size. In a recorded working session, an AIT engineer said that when the wireframe was viewed close to real screen size, the smaller text size was really small, and that a heat pump installer described as an old man with glasses might not be amused. The design response was to cut widget content to three pieces of information each.

The engagement also addressed rendering performance against a fast-spun rotary control. An AIT engineer said that users handle the rotary knob very quickly and that tile scrolling must also be fast. The design response was to remove the expensive interaction from the common case: equal-size widgets resized to the number of installed modes, so one to four modes fit with no horizontal scrolling, covering the overwhelming majority of installations.

Nothing in the AIT engagement was tested with users. The evidence supports design reasoning against physical size and control-speed constraints, not user-validated performance.

## MDU evidence from numbers read on a moving vessel

In the MDU engagement, the live Now value was removed from both motion cards because of how the number behaved in the condition in which it was read. The documented rationale was that a digit updating every second on a moving vessel cost attention and returned no useful value. The four numeric cells on each card became minimum, maximum, period and maximum velocity.

The roll display was drawn 1:1 up to approximately ±40–45° and then maxed out beyond that, like a speedometer. The design decision was based on the reader's actual situation rather than the full range of the data.

The MDU evidence has a clear limit. Nothing in the engagement was tested with users, and the system was never used at sea by the design team.

## Assemblio evidence from a client-stated shop-floor mismatch

In the Assemblio case, Creative Navy did not observe a shop floor. Every statement about the working environment is client-stated.

The documented mismatch was that the Smart Viewer was tuned for mouse navigation and used where there is no mouse. A light theme existed but was unfinished; the client described it as beta and work in progress. The light theme was the one the shop floor needed.

The Assemblio case is an example of an interface that works where it was built but not where it is used, with the evidence limited to the client's description of the working environment.

## Synthetic adversarial fixtures in KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group

In the KISPE Space engagement, the design scenario was deliberately adversarial rather than a happy path. At the scenario moment, the imagery feed was down, the newest image would not render, the highest-resolution image covered only part of the area, one image was restricted, the positioning fix was stale while the communications reading was current, and a predicted overflight had not happened yet.

This is rigour about reality rather than contact with it. The fixture was synthetic, nothing was tested with users, and nothing was evaluated on representative hardware.

In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, the scenario was also adversarial on purpose. At the scenario moment, one aircraft's link was degrading, its telemetry was ageing, a warning belonged to an aircraft not under command, the offline map was incomplete while reporting a completed download, and the planning estimate on screen belonged to a superseded revision.

The same limit applies. The fixture was synthetic, so the evidence is rigour about reality rather than contact with it. The product was built and is in test, not deployed; the documented evidence does not support any field, hardware, lighting, glove or vibration claim.

## Oceaneering evidence from reported depot context

In the Oceaneering engagement, the depot environment was described in interviews rather than observed by Creative Navy. A staff software engineer described hospitals as looking organised but not being organised, with vehicle areas that were quite dirty and with other things left standing around.

The floor was part of the interface in the predecessor system's reported context. Vehicles ran on dark flooring and people were directed to light flooring. Ceiling-mounted illuminated signs and speakers issued spoken instructions to clear the passage at intersections. Station positions were numbered on the floor, and send and receive roles were painted on the floor in the same colours used by the screen.

Operators did not consult the screen to collect an arrived cart. They walked in, saw the cart and took it without looking at the panel. The evidence is limited to reported interview context: Creative Navy visited no depot, observed no operator and measured nothing in this engagement.

## Handheld command-and-control glove finding from a client-run prototype session

In a prototype session run by the client for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them, six participants were former military personnel and current drone operators. Some worked bare-handed and some worked gloved.

The client-run prototype session found that gloved touch was unreliable on the target panel. The display did not consistently register gloved input, the gloves available were assessed as not well suited to the touchscreen, icons and terminology were reported as needing refinement, and the remainder was reported favourably.

This was not a usability test. No criteria were fixed in advance, there were no pass rules, no task times and no error counts. It was not Creative Navy's research, it was not validation of the design, and it tested a non-functional prototype rather than a system. The finding partially undercuts the premise of the sizing work.

## Maritime VTS evidence from control-room observation and sanitised-data testing

In the maritime VTS engagement, Creative Navy observed operators in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site, at a workstation matching the real configuration, and designed and tested against restricted networks, paired displays, day and night control-room conditions, dense traffic, stale feeds, interrupted sources and permission limits. Every evaluated task ran on sanitised data in a training or prototype configuration, never a live traffic position.

The validation fixtures included forty-eight targets with three traffic alerts, one equipment fault and two advisories. These are designed test conditions, not observations. The performance-in-reality claim must carry both halves together: observation occurred in working control rooms, while evaluated tasks used sanitised data in a training or prototype configuration.

## visioncheckout evidence from a performance claim failing in observed environments

In the visioncheckout case, the product is in development, nothing has shipped, and no outcome of the redesign exists. The case is not evidence of designing for real conditions; it is evidence of a performance claim not surviving contact with reality.

The demonstration claim was three seconds. Across 563 observed interactions in three operating environments, the measured durations for the system being replaced were 11 to 25 seconds. The field framing was one researcher, five days and six locations across three organisations, with durations measured by clock during observation.

The conditions producing the gap included overhead lighting that commonly cast a dark area on both the screen and the tray surface, one site that was simply dark, and installations where about 70cm separated the display and the user's head. The type-size specification had assumed shorter viewing distances and was answered by raising defaults rather than adding a mode. The largest single component of lost time was guests looking for their card.

## Evidence basis and limits of the concept

Performance in reality is supported by multiple evidence types in the documented case set. Some examples use real deployment data, live product analytics, field measurements or ecological testing. Other examples are more limited: synthetic fixtures, client-stated context, interview-reported context, client-run prototype findings, sanitised data or comprehension testing in a parked car.

The principle does not mean that every engagement includes field deployment, user testing or longitudinal measurement. It means that the design and evaluation standard is the condition that determines performance in the domain. Where the evidence does not reach that standard, the limitation must remain visible.

Results from controlled usability testing do not necessarily generalise to operational performance. The measurable consequence of designing for performance in reality is that results can be stated with specific evidential grounding only when they survive contact with real use.

## Related pages

Performance in reality is closely related to domain learning, because Creative Navy's documentation treats observed or reconstructed operational reality as necessary input for design decisions. It also connects to degraded mode, cognitive load, workflow robustness, operational clarity and state visibility, because these concepts describe conditions that often determine whether a system performs under real use.
